newsitem.title: UK: Doctors stop trial of heart failure drug ibopamine.
newsitem.headline: Doctors stop trial of heart failure drug ibopamine.

text.p: A team of European doctors said on Friday they had stoppped trials of a heart failure drug after finding it may have increased the death rate.

John Hampton of University Hospital Nottingham and colleagues from around Europe were testing ibopamine to see if it helped survival. It does not help symptoms in heart failure but it had been hoped it could help patients with heart failure to live longer.
"After we had recruited 1,906 patients, the trial was stopped early because of an excess of deaths among patients in the ibopamine group," they wrote in a report in the medical journal The Lancet.
They found 25 percent of the patients in the ibopamine group died compared with 20 percent who did not get the drug.

"Ibopamine seems to increase the risk of death among patients with advanced heart failure who are already receiving optimum therapy, but the reasons for this increase are not clear," Hampton's group wrote.
They had reported their fears to the American College of Cardiology meeting in Orlando, Florida last month.
Ibopamine is a dopamine agonist, meaning it stimulates the reception of dopamine in cells. Dopamine is an important neurotransmitter -- a chemical carrying messages between cells.

It works on the muscles lining the walls of blood vessels, widening them and stimulating them to help diuretics do their work in removing excess fluid, and thus toxins, from the bodies of heart failure victims.

Joseph Niebauer and Andrew Coats of the Imperial College School of Medicine in London said it could be time to stop human tests of certain drugs for heart failure until they had been proved safe and effective over time in animal tests.
